food.text: After the rationing of the Second World War, Elizabeth David's 1950 A Book of Mediterranean Food had wide influence. It brought the cuisines of that region, including Italy, into English homes. Her success encouraged other cookery writers to describe other styles, including Chinese and Thai cuisine.

Indian cuisine is the most popular alternative to traditional cooking in Britain, followed by Chinese and Italian food. In 2003, there were roughly 9,000 Indian restaurants in Britain. They accounted for two-thirds of all eating out and served about 2.5 million British customers every week.

French gastronomy was added by UNESCO to its lists of the world's intangible cultural heritage in November 2010. In the 20th century, culinary tourism and the Guide Michelin helped acquaint commoners with the bourgeois cuisine of urban elites and the peasant cuisine of the French countryside.
Chicken tikka masala was apparently invented in Glasgow in the early 1970s. By 2015, it was one of Britain's most popular dishes.

Beans on toast was already being eaten by the end of the 19th century. A marketing push by Heinz in 1927 made it a widely popular quick and cheap snack. Britain hosts the largest Heinz food processing plant in the world, and Britons eat more baked beans than any other country.

Six of Britain's ten three-star Michelin restaurants are in London alone, more than any other city in the world except for Paris and Tokyo. Writer Debora Robertson has argued that British cuisine has shed the spectres of wartime rationing and post-war food scarcity, and that its standards now rival those of France.

Immigration has reshaped French cooking. Couscous is often cited as one of modern France's most widely consumed dishes, and falafel, pho and banh mi have become popular. Roughly twenty-five percent of chefs in France are immigrants, and in Paris about half are.

Veeraswamy, founded in 1926, is the oldest surviving Indian restaurant in Britain. By the 1970s, over three-quarters of the Indian restaurants in the country were owned and run by people of Bangladeshi origin, mainly from the Sylhet area.
Balti cuisine was introduced to Britain in 1977 in Birmingham. Most Indian restaurants in Britain are run by entrepreneurs of Bangladeshi (often Sylhetis) and Pakistani origin.

Indian restaurants in Britain gradually moved beyond flock wallpaper and standardised menus. The Bombay Brasserie opened in Gloucester Road, London, in 1982, serving the kind of food actually eaten in India. In 2001, Tamarind and Zaika became two London Indian restaurants to gain Michelin stars.

The Fat Duck in Bray, a three-Michelin-star restaurant, was named the world's best restaurant in 2005. In 2010, The Waterside Inn, also in Bray, became the first restaurant outside of France to retain three Michelin stars for a quarter of a century.

Ratatouille began as a rural Provençal way of using surplus summer vegetables. No fully developed modern recipe appears in printed cookbooks before the late 19th or early 20th century, and a modern version does not appear in print until 1930. Later, the layered Confit byaldi reinterpreted it for haute cuisine.

In 2001, two Indian restaurants in London, Tamarind and Zaika, gained Michelin stars for the quality of their cooking. Tamarind opened in 1995 and Zaika in 1999. Earlier, the Bombay Brasserie, which opened in 1982, had been a pioneer in serving the kind of food actually eaten in India.
The number of Indian restaurants in Britain peaked at some 12,000 in 2015. It then decreased to some 8,000 by 2023.

During World War I's outbreak, the chef Escoffier renamed the sauce allemande, meaning 'German sauce', as sauce parisienne. He had perfected the sauce in the early 20th century. It shows how war touched even the names of dishes.

Paris's first Tex-Mex restaurant opened in March 1983, but business was slow. After the 1986 film Betty Blue showed characters drinking tequila shots and eating chili con carne, restaurateur Claude Benayoun said everybody in Paris wanted a shot of tequila and a bowl of chili.

art.text: In 2014 the moat of the Tower of London was filled with 888,246 ceramic red poppies, each representing one British or Colonial serviceman killed in World War I. The installation was called Blood Swept Lands and Seas of Red. An estimated 5 million people saw it.
art.source_title: Blood Swept Lands and Seas of Red
tags: Blood Swept Lands and Seas of Red

art.text: The first half of the 20th century in France saw the revolutionary experiments of Cubism, Dada and Surrealism. These movements had a major impact on western art and eventually on world art. After World War II, France's preeminence in the visual arts was progressively eclipsed by developments elsewhere, especially in the United States.

About 1,200 country houses have been demolished in England since 1900, and it has been estimated that one in six English country houses was lost during the 20th century. At the peak in 1955, a house was being lost every five days. Few people were particularly interested or bothered at the time.
art.source_title: Destruction of country houses in 20th-century Britain

art.text: The tourist-filled Tower installation was meant to be temporary. Despite calls from Prime Minister David Cameron and other politicians to extend it, Historic Royal Palaces and the artist Paul Cummins refused, saying transience was a key part of the artistic concept. The poppies were removed and distributed to their purchasers.
art.source_title: Blood Swept Lands and Seas of Red
tags: Blood Swept Lands and Seas of Red

art.text: In 1960 Pierre Restany and Yves Klein founded the New Realism movement in France. Its members sought to bring life and art closer together, and it has often been compared with Pop Art. Yves Klein had nude women roll around in blue paint and throw themselves at canvases.

Stockport War Memorial Art Gallery, built in 1925, was the town's principal memorial to those who died in the First World War, and its memorial hall has white marble plaques recording the names of 2,200 First World War casualties. Plaques were later added for those who died in the Second World War and later conflicts, including the Korean War, Falklands War, and The Troubles. James Theodore Halliday designed it in a Neoclassical Greek Revival style, and it was funded entirely by voluntary subscriptions. Prince Henry opened it on 15 October 1925.

In 1917, Duchamp presented a white porcelain urinal signed R. Mutt as a work of art at an art show in New York. This made him the father of the "readymade". Francis Picabia and Duchamp had been exploring similar notions at the time Dada began in Zurich.

About 17,500 volunteers planted the poppies at the Tower, overseen by stage designer Tom Piper and Yeoman Warder Jim Duncan. The last was planted on 11 November 2014 by a 13-year-old cadet, Harry Hayes. Members of the public could pre-order poppies for £25 each, with proceeds going to six service charities.
art.source_title: Blood Swept Lands and Seas of Red
tags: Blood Swept Lands and Seas of Red

art.text: Among the New Realists, Niki de Saint Phalle created bloated and vibrant plastic figures, and Arman gathered found objects into boxed or resin-coated assemblages. César Baldaccini made large compressed object-sculptures, and Daniel Spoerri used meals and food as artistic material.

In April 2016 the sculpture Weeping Window, part of the poppy installation, was installed at St Magnus Cathedral in Kirkwall, Orkney. It marked the 100th anniversary of the Battle of Jutland. It was part of a UK tour of the poppy sculptures Wave and Weeping Window that visited 19 locations.
art.source_title: Blood Swept Lands and Seas of Red
tags: Blood Swept Lands and Seas of Red

art.text: Ben Vautier was the most significant French artist of the Fluxus movement, which was named and loosely organized in 1962 by George Maciunas. Fluxus encouraged a do it yourself aesthetic and disparaged the market-driven art world. Vautier incorporated graffiti and found objects into his work.

war.text: Germany's strategy in 1914 was to quickly defeat France, but its advance was halted in September. The French offensive in Alsace-Lorraine had been a disastrous failure, with casualties exceeding 260,000, and by the end of 1914 Germany had inflicted 230,000 more casualties than it lost. The Western Front then solidified into a near-continuous line of fortified trenches, where barbed wire, machine guns and artillery made massed infantry advances extremely difficult and costly.
World War II is generally considered to have begun on 1 September 1939, when Nazi Germany under Adolf Hitler invaded Poland. The United Kingdom and France then declared war on Germany.

After the fall of France in June 1940, the war continued mainly between Germany, now assisted by Fascist Italy, and the British Empire and British Commonwealth. The fighting included the aerial Battle of Britain, the Blitz, and the naval Battle of the Atlantic.

The Cod Wars were a series of 20th-century confrontations between Iceland and the United Kingdom about fishing rights in the North Atlantic. British fishing boats were escorted by the Royal Navy, while the Icelandic Coast Guard used long hawsers to cut nets from them, and ships from both sides were damaged by ramming attacks. Men were hurt: in 1976 a Grimsby fisherman was seriously injured when a hawser hit him after Icelandic vessels cut a trawl. The only confirmed death came on 29 August 1973, when Halldór Hallfreðsson, an engineer on the Icelandic vessel Ægir, was electrocuted by his welding equipment after sea water flooded the compartment where he was repairing damage from a collision with the British frigate HMS Apollo.
In early August 1914, Germany declared war on Russia and France. The United Kingdom entered the war after Germany invaded Belgium.
British discontent over the Norwegian campaign led to the resignation of Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain. He was replaced by Winston Churchill on 10 May 1940.

The United Kingdom declared war on Germany on Sunday 3 September 1939, two days after the German invasion of Poland. Prime minister Neville Chamberlain announced the state of war to the British public in a radio broadcast at 11:00. France also declared war later the same day.
war.source_title: British declaration of war on Germany (1939)

war.text: In April 1917 the US Army had fewer than 300,000 men, compared with British and French armies of 4.1 and 8.3 million. By June 1918 over 667,000 members of the American Expeditionary Forces had been transported to France, and the figure reached 2 million by the end of November.

The First Cod War lasted from 1 September 1958 to 11 March 1961. It began as soon as a new Icelandic law came into force at midnight on 1 September 1958, expanding the Icelandic fishery zone from 4 to 12 nautical miles.
After Congress declared war on Germany on 6 April 1917, the US Navy sent a battleship group to Scapa Flow to join the Grand Fleet. It also provided convoy escorts.

The First Cod War ended with a settlement in late February 1961 after the United Nations Conference on the Law of the Sea. Iceland's 12 nautical mile limit was accepted, but Britain kept fishing rights in allocated zones in the outer 6 nautical miles for three years. The Icelandic Althing approved the agreement on 11 March 1961.

In January 1919 the Canadian government offered to transport all dependents of Canadian servicemen from Britain to Canada, with free ocean transport and rail passage. By the end of 1946, over forty thousand Canadian servicemen had married women from Europe.

literature.text: Agatha Christie, a 20th-century crime writer, is the best-selling novelist of all time. Her mystery novels are outsold only by Shakespeare and The Bible.
T. S. Eliot was born American but moved to Britain in 1914. He published The Waste Land in 1922. He is described as arguably the most important English-language poet of the 20th century.

Paris publishers issued English-language books that were banned in America. Sylvia Beach published James Joyce's Ulysses in Paris in 1922, and Olympia Press later published Lolita and Naked Lunch. France was seen as more permissive about censorship.

Several British Nobel laureates were immigrants. Doris Lessing came from Southern Rhodesia and published her first novel, The Grass Is Singing, in 1950. V. S. Naipaul was born in Trinidad, and Kazuo Ishiguro was born in Japan and moved to Britain with his parents at age 6.

Eliot's Four Quartets appeared between 1935 and 1942, some years after The Waste Land (1922). Free verse and other stylistic innovations came to the forefront in this era, and Eliot and Ezra Pound were especially associated with them.

Invasion literature grew into a genre of over 400 novels and stories by 1914. Several were written by or ghostwritten for military officers who believed the nation would be saved if their favoured tactic was adopted. The genre began in Britain with The Battle of Dorking in 1871.

David Jones, a London-Welsh poet and painter, wrote In Parenthesis. It was one of the very few experimental poems to come out of World War I. English poetry of the period also included modernists such as Hugh MacDiarmid, Mina Loy and Basil Bunting.

Paul Léautaud kept a monumental 13-volume diary, the Journal Littéraire, chronicling the Parisian literary world in the first half of the 20th century. Mavis Gallant called it the greatest study of character ever written. His biographer James Harding thought it more devastating in its truthfulness than Rousseau's Confessions.

Bloodaxe Books published The New Poetry in 1993, featuring Simon Armitage, Kathleen Jamie, Glyn Maxwell and others. In the 1980s and 1990s, poet-led organisations such as Torriano and Blue Nose Poets helped set the norms of grass-roots poetry workshops and readings across the UK.
Michael Moorcock edited England Invaded, published in 1977. It collected six popular invasion literature stories, reviving a genre that had flourished before the First World War.

Several French novels of the early 20th century followed older traditions. Romain Rolland's Jean-Christophe, published from 1906 to 1912, continued the roman-fleuve tradition inspired by Balzac and Zola. Popular taste stayed conservative, and Georges Feydeau's farces were widely enjoyed.

science.text: In England, the science content of the National Curriculum was expanded in the mid-2010s. The Key Stage 4 science version was first published in December 2014, and a GCSE combined science version followed in June 2015, first implemented in September 2016.

In 2023–24, 42150 students in England enrolled for physical science degrees in higher education. That was a little under half the 80085 who enrolled for biological science degrees, a gap that ties in with England's shortage of science teachers.
Jean Cavaillès (1903–1944) was a French philosopher of science who studied science, mathematical logic and set theory. He was also part of the French Resistance in World War II.
The larger GCSE science content triggered a change in the GCSE grading system in England. The old A*–G scale was replaced by a 9–1 scale.

Medicine, veterinary medicine, psychology and subjects allied to medicine made up 440430 enrolments in England in 2023–24. This dwarfs physical science enrolments, even when the 90870 engineering and technology enrolments are counted.

politics.text: Following the United Kingdom's declaration of war on Nazi Germany on 3 September 1939, numerous countries of the Empire and Commonwealth joined the Second World War. They included four of the five independent Dominions: Australia, Canada, South Africa and New Zealand. Together the Empire and Commonwealth held direct or de facto control of 25% of the world's population.
politics.source_title: British Empire in World War II

politics.text: From World War II until 2017, French politics was dominated by two opposed groupings. One was left-wing: the French Section of the Workers' International, succeeded by the Socialist Party in 1969. The other was the right-wing Gaullist Party.
tags: French Section of the Workers' International

politics.text: In the 2017 presidential and legislative elections, the radical centrist party La République En Marche! became the dominant force in France, overtaking both Socialists and Republicans. Its opponent in the second round of the 2017 and 2022 presidential elections was the growing far-right party National Rally.

On 16 January 1968, a few weeks after the devaluation of the pound, Prime Minister Harold Wilson and Defence Secretary Denis Healey announced a British withdrawal from major bases East of Suez. Troops were to leave primarily Malaysia and Singapore by the end of 1971, instead of 1975 as earlier planned.

From September 1939 to mid-1942, the UK led Allied efforts in multiple global military theatres. Commonwealth, Colonial and Imperial Indian forces, totalling close to 15 million serving men and women, fought the German, Italian, Japanese and other Axis armies, air-forces and navies. The cost was 150,000 military deaths, 400,000 wounded, 100,000 prisoners, over 300,000 civilian deaths, and the loss of 70 major warships, 39 submarines, 3,500 aircraft, 1,100 tanks and 65,000 vehicles.
politics.source_title: British Empire in World War II

politics.text: After the Suez Crisis, Britain again deployed its armed forces in the Middle East, intervening in Oman in 1957, Jordan in 1958 and Kuwait in 1961. This time it had American approval, since the new Prime Minister Harold Macmillan's foreign policy was to remain firmly aligned with the United States.

A guerrilla war waged by the Greek Cypriot organisation EOKA against British rule ended in 1959 with the London and Zürich Agreements. Cyprus was granted independence in 1960. The UK kept the military bases of Akrotiri and Dhekelia as sovereign base areas.
Britain's war budget included £2.7 billion borrowed from the Empire's Sterling Area, which Britain eventually paid back.
politics.source_title: British Empire in World War II

politics.text: In 2022, the New Ecological and Social People's Union was the second-largest voting block elected to France's lower house. Right-wing populist National Rally became the largest opposition party in the National Assembly that year. Since 2020, The Ecologists have also performed well in mayoral elections in major cities.

The French Gaullist Party changed its name repeatedly. It became the Rally of the French People (1947), the Union of Democrats for the Republic (1958), the Rally for the Republic (1976), the Union for a Popular Movement (2007) and The Republicans (since 2015).

philosophy.text: In The Myth of Sisyphus (1942), Albert Camus states what he considers the fundamental question of philosophy: is suicide the correct response to an absurd world? His answer is "No. It requires revolt." He concludes that one must imagine Sisyphus happy.

Simone Weil was an Alsatian Jewish mystic philosopher and political activist. Her book The Need for Roots was published posthumously in 1949. Her ideas included uprootedness, decreation, and the view that obligations are the basis of rights.

Since the 20th century, British philosophy has been dominated by analytic philosophy, which includes G. E. Moore and Bertrand Russell. The Philosophical Society of England was founded in 1913 and publishes The Philosopher.

Albert Camus won the 1957 Nobel Prize in Literature but rejected being labelled an existentialist, preferring to be called an absurdist. His novel The Stranger (1942) was ranked the greatest book of the 20th Century by Le Monde.
Philosopher of science Jean Cavaillès, born in 1903, studied science, mathematical logic and set theory. He was part of the French Resistance in World War II and died in 1944.

Philippa Foot defended naturalist moral realism and introduced the famous "trolley problem" into ethical discourse. She is one of three thinkers, with Elizabeth Anscombe and Alasdair Macintyre, credited with sparking a revival of Aristotle's virtue ethics.
Antony Flew notably converted to Christianity from atheism. Recent British philosophers have been particularly active in the philosophy of religion, and John Hick advocated religious pluralism.
The French philosopher Gaston Bachelard (1884–1962) introduced the concepts of epistemological obstacle and epistemological break. Both are ideas within the French philosophy of science tradition.

Simone Weil described decreation as renouncing the gift of free will. She also believed compassion involved attention, was patriotic, and must act in the area of metaxy. Her influence reached Pope Paul VI and René Girard.

Gaston Bachelard introduced the concepts of epistemological obstacle and epistemological break into French philosophy of science. Georges Canguilhem, meanwhile, reintroduced vitalism into the philosophy of biology.

Elizabeth Anscombe wrote Intention (1957), a monograph with an influential treatment of action. Her 1958 article "Modern Moral Philosophy" criticized consequentialism. Alasdair Macintyre later contributed After Virtue (1981) to the virtue ethics revival.
Georges Canguilhem (1904–1995) reintroduced vitalism into the philosophy of biology. He was one of several French thinkers who shaped how science itself was understood in the 20th century.

The French reception of Hegel in the 1930s and 1940s, particularly through the lectures of Alexandre Kojève and the work of Jean Hyppolite, established a "Hegelian paradigm" that shaped much of post-war thought. Kojève's focus on the master-slave dialectic led to a reading of Hegel that emphasized conflict, negation, and death. Combined with the historical experience of totalitarianism, this led to an association of Hegel's philosophy with the logic of totalizing state power, a view articulated in different ways by Levinas, Bataille and Sartre.

Graham Priest advocates dialetheism, the view that the law of non contradiction is false. He also defends noneism, a belief in nonexistent objects, and wrote An Introduction to Non-Classical Logic (2001).
Jules Vuillemin (1920–2001) focused on epistemology and introduced the "philosophy of algebra". His work belongs to the French tradition that also produced Cavaillès's studies of mathematical logic.

culture.text: France hosts the annual cycling race Tour de France, described as the world's biggest annual sporting event. Other popular sports there include football, judo, tennis, rugby union and pétanque. The country has also hosted the 1938 and 1998 FIFA World Cups.

In 2013, France legalised same-sex marriage. The law, called "Marriage pour tous" ("marriage for all"), was passed in April 2013 and validated by the Conseil constitutionnel in May 2013. The first French same-sex marriage took place on 29 May 2013 in Montpellier.

The Welsh Church Act 1914 separated the four Church of England dioceses in Wales from the rest of the Church and disestablished it. The Act came into operation in 1920. Since then there has been no established church in Wales.

Since 1923, France has been famous for the 24 Hours of Le Mans sports car endurance race. The Stade de France in Saint-Denis is the country's largest stadium. It hosted the finals of the 1998 FIFA World Cup and the 2007 Rugby World Cup.

George Orwell's eleven rules for making tea appear in his essay "A Nice Cup of Tea". It was published in the London Evening Standard on 12 January 1946. Orwell also documented working class life in northern England in The Road to Wigan Pier (1937).

Between 2014 and 2018, Historic England ran the First World War Memorials Programme to mark the centenary of the First World War. Some 2,500 additional war memorials were listed, and a number of previously listed memorials were upgraded to Grade I.
culture.source_title: Grade I listed buildings in England completed in the 20th century
